original.target_description: Experiment 1: decision-makers’ average proportion of together choices tested against chance level in the costly joint-action task.

n.sample_role: Decision-makers, one per pair (40 participants in 20 pairs overall).
n.exclusions: No participants excluded; 1.5% trial exclusions described for trial-time analysis.
n.quote: We recruited 20 pairs in total (40 participants) ... The roles of decision-maker and partner were randomly assigned. ... No participants were excluded.

replication.target_description: Replication of Curioni et al. Experiment 1: 50 Decision-makers in 50 pairs, mean proportion of together choices versus 50% chance, two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Separate devices 3.05 m apart.

n.sample_role: Decision-makers, one per human pair; 100 participants in 50 pairs overall.
n.exclusions: No participant or choice-data exclusions are reported; analytic count identified from the 50 pairs and one Decision-maker per pair, rather than treating the overall 100 as analytic n.
n.location: pp. 3–4, Method: Participants and Procedure; p. 7, Data analysis: Choice data
n.quote: A sample of 100 undergraduate and graduate students at McMaster University (50 human pairs, Mage = 18.51 years, SD = 2.01) participated in the experiment. ... Within each pair, one participant performed the task in the role of the “Decision-maker” and the other in the role of the “Helper”.

reported_success.quote: Our failure to replicate a preference for joint action even when it is more costly was surprising given the robustness of this effect across multiple experiments in Curioni et al. (2022).

notes: Original title and DOI verified in Europe PMC full text. The supplied replication reference is an OSF preregistration; the supplied preprint URL resolves to Preferences for costly cooperation are highly individualized (Lalli et al.). Its Method explicitly links preregistration 10.17605/OSF.IO/EVDP5 and identifies this as a replication of Curioni et al. Experiment 1; the target result is on the supplied p. 11. Printed effect metrics and precision retained. Sample roles distinguish Decision-makers from total participants.
